impact.location_description: Northeast Pacific Ocean, roughly several hundred km off the California coast
impact.context: Open ocean, no possibility of meteorite recovery.

sensor_detections: US government satellite sensors, 0.15 kt at 30.0N 136.0W
confirmation.eyewitness: None documented; remote ocean location far from shore.

scientific_results: Like 2019 MO, 2024 UQ was recognized as a genuine impactor only after the GOES/sensor flash appeared -- a retrospective search of Catalina Sky Survey (station 703) images then found a faint precovery detection about an hour before the credited ATLAS discovery, extending and firming up the fit after the fact.

At 21 km/s, it tied 2024 RW1 for the fastest entry velocity in the 13-object set, illustrating that short-warning cases cluster at both extremes of encounter geometry (very slow grazing entries like 2026 RW1, and fast steep ones like this).

The case reinforced, alongside 2019 MO, that at very short arcs (here about 8-9 observations from 2 stations, U=7) the automated Scout/Meerkat hazard-assessment pipelines can correctly rate an object as an imminent impactor but real-world confirmation of identity still depends on catching a second, independent detection -- sensor, precovery, or both.
narrative: ATLAS's Haleakala telescope picked up 2024 UQ at 09:08 UTC on 22 October 2024; with only about 1.8 hours of warning, follow-up was minimal before the object entered the atmosphere at 10:54:48 UTC over the northeast Pacific, disintegrating at about 38 km altitude and releasing roughly 0.15 kt, recorded by a GOES lightning-mapper flash and US government sensors. A subsequent search of Catalina Sky Survey imagery turned up a faint detection roughly an hour before the ATLAS tracklet began, improving the orbit solution after the fact. With no meteorites possible over open ocean and no eyewitnesses, 2024 UQ -- like 2019 MO five years earlier -- became one of the two cases in the 13-object set where the fireball evidence effectively did the confirming, rather than advance tracking alone.
